Hi there,

I build DanteWorks, a Shopify app that turns supplier order confirmations into draft products, so I have a stake here. But I also ran a fashion store, so here are the real-world cases that broke our imports, in case they help your matching rules:

  • Size matrices: sizes as columns, quantities in the cells, “-” meaning “not ordered”. A naive import creates the full size run instead of only the sizes ordered.
  • Same size on two lines: one line per delivery date, same SKU and size. They need to be summed, not flagged as duplicates.
  • Colour hidden in the SKU suffix (e.g. 540-19643-30 = olive, -50 = navy), with no colour column at all.
  • Same reference, two different products (same style code, different fabric and price). Matching on SKU alone merges them.
  • Two references for one product: the same style split by size range across two lines.
  • Gross vs net price: “75.00 / -16% / 63.00”. The retail price must be based on the 75, not the 63, and a checker that only compares one price column misses it.
  • UK/US sizes on the supplier side, EU in the store, and the conversion depends on the brand.
  • Non-product lines that look like products: shipping, deposits, carton sections that re-list the items.

+1 to @YangCommerceOps: anything uncertain should be shown with the exact excerpt from the supplier file and confirmed by a human, never guessed.

Reading through this thread, the examples @Remyleft shared about size matrices and SKU suffixes really stood out. With apparel imports, I’ve found that the bigger problems usually come from the way the supplier structures the data, not from simple typos.

When I’m getting supplier files ready for Shopify, especially with a lot of variants, I usually run through a few checks first:

  1. Flatten the size matrix properly: If sizes are listed across columns with quantities underneath, it’s easy for an importer to create every possible size as a variant. I’d filter out the zero-quantity ones first so you don’t end up with a bunch of dead variants.

  2. Combine split delivery dates: If the same SKU appears on multiple rows because quantities are arriving at different times, add those quantities together before importing. Otherwise, you can end up with Shopify taking the last row’s quantity instead of the actual total.

  3. Keep supplier discounts separate: I’d keep the normal wholesale price separate from any temporary discounted price. Using a one-off promo price as your Cost Per Item can throw off your margin history later.

  4. Do a dry run on the weird stuff: Before importing anything into the live store, I’d test SKUs where things like color or size are buried in the SKU itself, such as -BLK-M. That’s usually where a mapping script can quietly go wrong.

Having a quick staging checklist for these things saves a lot of headaches later. It’s much easier to catch a bad mapping before the import than to clean up hundreds of incorrect variants afterward.

I think the main question is what this does that a spreadsheet comparison doesn’t already do pretty easily.

If I have the supplier’s original file and the Shopify CSV, Excel/Google Sheets can already flag missing SKUs, price differences, mismatched variants, etc. with lookups or Power Query. And if this is something I do repeatedly, I’d probably build that comparison once and reuse it.

So for me, the $19 wouldn’t really be the issue. The tool would need to make the process significantly easier than just comparing the two files — especially dealing intelligently with suppliers whose spreadsheets don’t use the same structure or naming conventions as Shopify.

If I could drop in basically any supplier spreadsheet and a Shopify CSV and it automatically figured out the mapping and gave me a clean exception report without setup, that would be much more interesting.

The #1 issue I see with supplier files is SKU mismatch — suppliers use their own codes with different casing, spaces, or dashes, so a straight comparison against your Shopify export fails even when the products match. Normalize both sides first (uppercase, strip spaces and dashes) and your match rate usually jumps from ~60% to ~95%.

Second trap: suppliers often list color-size as one row while Shopify splits variants into separate rows, so naive row-count comparisons break. Always compare at the SKU level, not the product level.

One column group I haven’t seen in this thread yet, and it’s the one that causes real trouble for clothing stores selling into the EU: fiber composition.

What I’d check in every supplier file before import:

  • Percentages add up to 100, for each component. A jacket with a lining needs the shell and the lining listed separately.
  • Fiber names from the EU list in Annex I of Regulation 1007/2011. Supplier files often say “Spandex” or “Lycra”. The EU name is elastane. “Cotton blend” or “poly mix” isn’t a composition at all.
  • Fibers in descending order by weight.
  • A translation for every country you sell to. The composition has to be in that country’s official language and visible on the product page before purchase (Article 16 of the same regulation).

What makes this checkable is keeping the composition in its own fields instead of the description text: one entry per fiber with its percentage, grouped by component. Then a missing or odd value shows up in the same check as a changed SKU or price.

It pays off again later. The JRC study on what the EU textile passport should contain (May 2026) lists fiber composition and care instructions among the proposed product data, so the same fields will feed the passport.

Disclosure: we build Mapasso, a DPP app for Shopify.
